new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (139 pp., LibreOffice-produced, intact text; the PDF's metadata confirms 139 pages, 1,015,726 bytes = the 991.92 KB attachment listed on the SIL archive record 91825). Printed p. 5 = PDF page 11: section "1.5 Stress" reads exactly "Stress is predictable. The penultimate vowel in a word is stressed, with secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels. It is realized as a somewhat lengthened vowel." followed by the two examples baguna 'garden' [bɑ.ˈɡu.nɑ] and fwayafwaya 'ground' [ˌfʷɑ.jɑ.ˈfʷɑ.jɑ] — verbatim as reported. Printed p. 3 (p. 9), section 1.3, has the diphthong caveat verbatim ("And it may affect syllable type and stress as examples below. au.na 'his/her uncle' [ˈɑu.nɑ] / a.u…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and falls on the penultimate vowel (syllable) of the word; diphthongs (V + higher V within a morpheme, plus /iu/) count as one syllable, so au.na 'his uncle' is [ˈɑu.nɑ] but a.u.na 'I carried' is [ɑ.ˈu.nɑ] (§1.3 p. 3). Stress is cued mainly by slight vowel lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels, i.e. every second syllable leftward from the penult (fwayafwaya [ˌfʷɑ.jɑ.ˈfʷɑ.jɑ]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Only caveat: whether a vowel sequence is a diphthong or two syllables changes which vowel is penultimate (§1.3 p. 3).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word ('in a word'); examples are single citation-form words, including a reduplicated form. No statement on phrase-level prominence. Fn. 1 p. 2 says the phonology chapter derives mainly from the Kaninuwa OPD revised in 2006.
new_statements.identity_note: Park & Park 2021 describe Kaninuwa [wat] as spoken in Sivesive (and hamlets) and Kikwanauta on the north coast of Goodenough Island, ~800 speakers — this is Glottolog kani1281 (alt. names Wataluma, Kaokao). Kassell 2012 reports no clear dialect boundaries, so no dialect qualification is needed. Lithgow 1976 refers to the same language as 'Wataluma'.

sources.note: §1.5 Stress, p. 5: stress is predictable, on the penultimate vowel of the word, with secondary stress on preceding alternate vowels, realized as slight lengthening; examples baguna [bɑ.ˈɡu.nɑ], fwayafwaya [ˌfʷɑ.jɑ.ˈfʷɑ.jɑ]. §1.3 p. 3 adds that diphthong vs. two-vowel-sequence analysis affects stress placement (au.na 'his uncle' [ˈɑu.nɑ] vs a.u.na 'I carried' [ɑ.ˈu.nɑ]). Fn. 1 p. 2 says the phonology chapter comes mainly from a Kaninuwa OPD revised in 2006. sources.note: Nothing on stress. Kaninuwa appears as 'Wataluma': p. 170 lists it among languages 'of which nothing is recorded, except survey material'; pp. 455, 460, 468, 478, 517 give location (two villages, north Goodenough), lexicostatistics (51% with Iduna, 44% Bwaidoka, 42% Are) and possessive/subject affix comparisons. Open mirror at sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/.
